No-read rate (bag diverted to manual encode): Corvane tags issued at Harlow Bay in August (Brackwater stock) 1.5%; issued Sep–Oct (Fennick stock) 11.8%, of which counters 11.5% and kiosks 12.0%. Corvane transfer tags issued at other stations 1.4%; Pelion tags 1.3%. Transfer and Pelion rates stay within 0.3 points on every array, including array 3 before and after its 3 Sep realignment. 14–16 Oct: Fennick stock ran short and counters 1–12 used Brackwater stock from stores; those tags failed at 1.6%, while kiosk tags issued the same days failed at 12.1%. Rhee): sampled no-read images show faint, broken bars; the images cannot show whether the media or the printer heat setting is responsible."},{"id":"C10","stage":"S1","title":"Interview notes with three Tessaly evening-bank crew leads, 7 Nov","source":"Corvane quality officer","sourceType":"staff-account","text":"All three leads said the evening bank has been 'tight' since the two new departures and that they are short by one or two loaders on some nights. 1 September four things changed at Harlow Bay at once. Tessaly Ground replaced Quillon as handler for both Corvane and Pelion. Corvane added two evening departures. Kiosk printer cleaning moved to fortnightly. And Corvane procurement switched every Harlow Bay counter and kiosk from Brackwater to cheaper Fennick tag stock. Corvane's departing mishandling rate rose from 4.1 to 7.6–7.9 per 1,000 passengers, and management blamed Tessaly's inexperienced crews. In fact, Fennick-printed tags fail automatic reading at about 12%, against about 1.5% for every other tag passing through the same arrays. When counters briefly went back to Brackwater stock (14–16 Oct), their no-read rate fell to 1.6% while kiosks still on Fennick stayed at 12%. The roughly six-fold rise in bags diverted to the unchanged two-person manual encode desk stretched evening dwell to about half an hour. Encode-path bags therefore reached laterals after closure and missed their flights. Corvane's auto-read bags showed no rise, and neither did Pelion's bags, which are worked by the same Tessaly crew pool. It is still unresolved whether Fennick stock is defective or simply needs different printer heat settings. The right step is to go back to Brackwater stock now. Penalising Tessaly would punish the wrong party.","answers":[{"itemId":"I1","expected":"contradicted","weight":3,"requiredEvidence":["C4"],"allowedEvidence":["E1","E2","E3","E4","E6","C4","C9","C1","C3","C10","C11","C16"],"tags":["leadership-narrative","misleading-signal","contrast-case","confounded"],"rationale":"The initial file fits H1 well: the timing matches, 41% of staff are new, and both the manager and the VP blame the handler. C4 refutes it. Pelion moved to Tessaly on the same date, is worked by the same single crew pool, and its rate stayed flat (3.6–3.8). Corvane's auto-read bags, which crews load the same way, also stayed flat (3.9→3.7). The whole excess sits in encode-path bags, and 91% of those reached the lateral after its scheduled closing time, so they arrived too late for any crew to load them."},{"itemId":"I2","expected":"supported","weight":3,"requiredEvidence":["C4","C9"],"allowedEvidence":["E4","E5","C4","C9","C3","C10","C12"],"tags":["less-salient-cause","cross-domain","natural-experiment"],"rationale":"C9 shows the no-read rise is confined to Fennick-stock tags (11.8%), across both counters and kiosks. Other tags on the same arrays read normally, and the 14–16 Oct reversion to Brackwater brought counter tags back to 1.6%. C4 shows the resulting six-fold increase in encode-diverted bags, longer dwell, and encode-path bags arriving after lateral closure, while auto-read bags were unaffected. Together they establish the full chain. Neither item alone does: C4 cannot say why no-reads rose, and C9 cannot say that no-reads explain the missed flights."},{"itemId":"I3","expected":"contradicted","weight":1,"requiredEvidence":["C4"],"allowedEvidence":["E4","C4","C6","C10"],"tags":["confounded","rival-change"],"rationale":"If schedule compression were the cause, it would hit all evening bags, including auto-read ones. C4 shows Corvane's auto-read mishandling flat. The rise is confined to encode-path bags, whose volume rose from 70 to 455–470 a day while passengers fell, which two extra departures cannot explain. Check-in timing of encode-path bags matches auto-read bags."},{"itemId":"I4","expected":"contradicted","weight":2,"requiredEvidence":["C9"],"allowedEvidence":["C9","C5","C4"],"tags":["misleading-signal","equipment-trap"],"rationale":"C5's array repairs in September invite this explanation. But C9 shows transfer and Pelion tags reading at 1.3–1.4% within 0.3 points on every array, including array 3 before and after realignment, and Brackwater-stock tags read normally in October. Failing scanners would affect all tags."},{"itemId":"I5","expected":"unknown","weight":2,"requiredEvidence":["E5","C9"],"allowedEvidence":["E5","C9","C7","C8"],"tags":["vendor-account","unresolved-mechanism"],"rationale":"Printer configuration was unchanged (E5), and Fennick stock fails on the same printers where Brackwater stock works (C9). That fits either a stock defect or a stock that needs higher printer heat. C9's engineer says the images cannot tell which. C7 (the supplier's own certificate, an interested source) and C8 (generic guidance) do not test the question. The claim is live but not established."},{"itemId":"I6","expected":"contradicted","weight":2,"requiredEvidence":["C4"],"allowedEvidence":["E1","E3","C4","C9","C11","C16"],"tags":["contrast-case","leadership-narrative"],"rationale":"The evidence counts against the link itself. The same handler changeover, on the same date and with the same crews, left Pelion's rate flat and Corvane's auto-read rate flat. The excess bags missed flights because they reached the lateral after closure, which is not a crew loading failure. The C11 cause codes favouring 'failure to load' are assigned before tracing and are rarely checked against the definition."},{"itemId":"I7","expected":"causal","weight":2,"requiredEvidence":["C9"],"allowedEvidence":["E5","C9","C5"],"tags":["natural-experiment"],"rationale":"Temporal order (switch on 1 Sep), specificity (only Fennick-range tags, at both counters and kiosks), the main rivals ruled out (same arrays read other tags normally; counters were not on the kiosk cleaning change) and a reversal (Brackwater at counters 14–16 Oct gave 1.6% while Fennick kiosks gave 12.1%) together establish causation."},{"itemId":"I8","expected":"causal","weight":2,"requiredEvidence":["C4"],"allowedEvidence":["C4","C9","E4","C3","C10","C12"],"tags":["mechanism"],"rationale":"Encode-diverted volume rose about six-fold, evening dwell rose from 7 to about 30 minutes, and 91% of the missed encode-path bags reached the lateral after scheduled closing. The encode-path mishandling rate rose from 0.2 to 3.8–4.2 while auto-read stayed flat. Check-in timing matches across paths, which rules out late check-in as a confounder."},{"itemId":"I9","expected":"association-only","weight":1,"requiredEvidence":["E5"],"allowedEvidence":["E5","C14","C7"],"tags":["confounded","side-issue"],"rationale":"Jam tickets rose from the same week the stock changed, so the two are associated. But kiosk preventive cleaning was halved on the same date, tickets are not split between kiosks and counters, and C14 records no cause for most callouts and no stock type. Causation is not established."},{"itemId":"I10","expected":"harmful","weight":2,"requiredEvidence":["C4","C9"],"allowedEvidence":["E2","E6","C4","C9","C13"],"tags":["punish-wrong-party","leadership-narrative"],"rationale":"With H1 contradicted, a breach notice and fee withholding punish a handler whose crews are not causing the rise. It also starts a cure and retender process (C13) and leaves the tag problem untouched. It is damaging under H2 whichever way H5 turns out."},{"itemId":"I11","expected":"preferred","weight":2,"requiredEvidence":["E5","C9"],"allowedEvidence":["E5","C4","C9","C7","C8"],"tags":["reversible-fix"],"rationale":"The October reversion showed Brackwater stock reads normally on the current printers. About five weeks of stock is in stores and the contract runs to 31 Dec (E5). Switching back removes the excess no-reads at source whether or not Fennick stock is defective, and it is easily reversed."},{"itemId":"I12","expected":"premature","weight":2,"requiredEvidence":["C9"],"allowedEvidence":["C7","C8","C9","E5"],"tags":["unconfirmed-hypothesis","vendor-account"],"rationale":"A defect claim would be justified if H5 were confirmed. But the evidence cannot yet separate defective stock from a printer-heat mismatch. If H5 is wrong, the claim is simply rejected and nothing lasting is lost."},{"itemId":"I13","expected":"acceptable","weight":1,"requiredEvidence":["C4"],"allowedEvidence":["C4","C12","E4"],"tags":["mitigation"],"rationale":"Extra encode capacity would shorten evening dwell and reduce misses, so it is reasonable. But it treats the symptom, needs HBAA's cooperation, and becomes unnecessary once the stock is switched back. That makes it reasonable, not best."},{"itemId":"I14","expected":"sufficient","weight":2,"requiredEvidence":["C4","C9"],"allowedEvidence":["E5","C4","C9"],"tags":["sufficiency"],"rationale":"With C4 and C9, the chain from Fennick stock to no-reads to encode backlog to missed flights is established, including a natural experiment. That is enough to commit to switching back to Brackwater stock. The open question in H5 does not affect that decision."}],"discriminatingReads":["C4","C9"],"lowValueReads":["C2","C13","C15"],"optimalReadPath":["C4","C9"],"authoringNotes":"Trap: everything changed on 1 Sep, and leadership claims only the handler changed (E6). E4 and E5 quietly contradict that, which keeps the case fair. C4 is the contrast case: Pelion, with the same handler, crews and date, stayed flat, and Corvane's auto-read path stayed flat. Only C4 settles H1, H3, R1, R3 and A1. C9 is the only item that ties no-reads to the tag stock, rules out the scanners and includes a reversal; it settles R2 and H4. Neither item alone supports H2. Distractors: C5 (array repairs, a lure towards H4), C11 (pre-trace cause codes favouring 'failure to load'), C10 and C3 (mixed staff and handler accounts), C16 (Tessaly's own figures elsewhere), C7 and C8 (interested or generic vendor material that leaves H5 open), C12 (encode staffing, relevant to A4 only), C14 (does not resolve R4). Reviewer checks: H5 stays unknown because no catalogue item independently tests the stock at adjusted heat settings. R4 stays association-only because the cleaning change has the same date and the tickets are not split between kiosks and counters. A4 is not preferred because switching the stock back removes the backlog at source within days. No action other than A2 is keyed preferred. All numbers reconcile: E1 and C4 match, and C4's routing split sums to the totals."}}

case.title: Harlow Bay: the bag rate that doubled the month the handler changed
case.setting: Harlow Bay International is a mid-sized fictional airport. Its baggage handling system and manual encode desk are run by the Harlow Bay Airport Authority (HBAA). Corvane Air is the largest carrier at the station. On 1 September Corvane's ramp handling, and Pelion Airways' ramp handling, moved from Quillon Ramp Services to Tessaly Ground. Departing bags pass through automatic tag reader arrays. Bags whose tags cannot be read are diverted to a manual encode desk and then sent on to the make-up laterals, where handler crews load carts that close 35 minutes before departure.
case.presentingRequest: Corvane's VP Ground Operations plans to issue Tessaly Ground a formal breach notice this Friday. Before that, the steering group has asked you to work out why Corvane's departing-bag mishandling rate at Harlow Bay nearly doubled from September and to recommend what to do next.

initialEvidence.source: Corvane Air station performance dashboard, Harlow Bay, extract dated 4 Nov
initialEvidence.text: Departing bags not carried on the booked flight, per 1,000 departing passengers: Jun 4.0, Jul 4.1, Aug 4.1, Sep 7.6, Oct 7.9. Departing passengers: Jun 205,000; Jul 212,000; Aug 219,000; Sep 188,000; Oct 176,000. Corvane network average excluding Harlow Bay: between 3.9 and 4.2 in every month. On-time departures within 15 minutes: Aug 81%, Sep 77%, Oct 78%. Annotation by station office: 'Ground handling transferred from Quillon Ramp Services to Tessaly Ground, 1 Sep.' No other annotations on the dashboard.

initialEvidence.source: Email from Dana Orlov, Corvane Station Manager, to Martin Achterberg, 5 Nov
initialEvidence.text: Martin, the rate sat at about 4 for over a year under Quillon and nearly doubled the month Tessaly took over. Their crews are green. I have personally watched bags sitting on a lateral with nobody working the cart. Tessaly keep blaming 'the airport system' and the encode desk, but that is the same desk Quillon worked with for six years without complaint. The two new evening departures add some pressure, but we ran heavier banks every summer. I recommend a formal breach notice and withholding the performance element of the fee until the rate is back under 4.5. Dana

initialEvidence.source: Tessaly Ground monthly staffing return to Corvane, 31 Oct
initialEvidence.text: Harlow Bay ramp headcount: 164 (contract minimum 160). Staff with under six months' airside experience: 67 (41%). Comparator from Quillon's final return, 31 Aug: headcount 152, of whom 18 (12%) had under six months. 23 former Quillon loaders transferred to Tessaly. Shift fill rate, Sep–Oct: early 97%, late 94%, evening 89%. Crewing model: a single Harlow Bay crew pool covers all Tessaly-handled turns (Corvane Air and Pelion Airways), assigned by the shift lead. Tessaly also staffs Corvane's baggage service desk under the same contract.

initialEvidence.source: Minutes, Corvane–Tessaly weekly operations review, 29 Oct
initialEvidence.text: Present: D. Orlov (Corvane), P. Venn (Tessaly ops lead), two Corvane duty managers. HBAA was invited but did not attend. 1. Mishandling: P. Venn said 'a lot of our late bags come down from the manual encode station after the lateral has closed' and asked Corvane to raise encode delays with HBAA. D. Orlov replied that the encode desk is unchanged and that crews should sweep laterals before closing carts. 2. Schedule: Corvane 418 and Corvane 422 added to the evening bank from 1 Sep; no change to lateral closing times. 3. Actions: Tessaly to submit a crew retraining plan by 12 Nov; Corvane to circulate the October dashboard.

initialEvidence.source: Corvane IT helpdesk ticket summary, bag-tag printers, Harlow Bay, 1 Aug–31 Oct
initialEvidence.text: Weekly tickets categorised 'tag printer jam/misfeed' (kiosks and counters combined): August weekly average 5; September–October weekly average 13. Context notes appended by helpdesk: (a) Procurement (L. Sato): from 1 Sep all Harlow Bay counters and kiosks switched from Brackwater Print tag stock to Fennick Labels stock under a new contract, unit cost down 18%. The Brackwater contract remains valid to 31 Dec, and about five weeks of Brackwater stock is held in station stores. (b) The kiosk maintenance vendor moved kiosk printer preventive cleaning from weekly to fortnightly from 1 Sep; counter printers are maintained by Corvane IT, schedule unchanged. (c) No printer configuration changes recorded since June.

initialEvidence.source: Message from Martin Achterberg, Corvane VP Ground Operations, to the Harlow Bay steering group, 6 Nov
initialEvidence.text: I've read Dana's note and I agree with it. We changed one thing on 1 September, the handler, and the mishandling rate nearly doubled. Tessaly bid low, staffed up with new hires, and is now pointing at the airport's IT. I want a breach notice drafted for my signature by Friday and the performance payment held. If anyone has evidence that this is not a handling problem, bring it to me before then. Otherwise we proceed.

catalogue.title: Tessaly Ground training and certification records, Harlow Bay ramp staff, Sep–Oct
catalogue.source: Tessaly Ground HR / Corvane quality audit
catalogue.text: All 164 ramp staff hold current airside passes and loading certification. The 67 staff with under six months' experience completed Tessaly's five-day ramp course and at least ten supervised turns before being rostered solo. Nine staff are overdue a 12-month refresher module, all of them ex-Quillon transfers. Two recordable bag-handling incidents in Sep–Oct (a bag dropped at a hold door; a cart overturned in wind), neither involving a lost bag. Corvane quality audited the training records on 20 Oct: no major findings.

catalogue.title: Corvane customer complaints and delayed-baggage compensation, Harlow Bay departures, Aug–Oct
catalogue.text: Delayed-baggage complaints from passengers departing Harlow Bay: Aug 312, Sep 588, Oct 611. Interim-expense compensation paid: Aug €21,400; Sep €44,900; Oct €47,300. Typical complaint narratives: the bag arrived on the next day's flight, and destination agents said it 'was left at Harlow Bay'. Twelve complaints mention rude staff at Harlow Bay check-in. Median delay before the bag reached the passenger: 26 hours, unchanged from August.

catalogue.title: Tessaly Ground internal ramp audit reports, Harlow Bay, Sep–Oct
catalogue.text: 48 turn audits. Procedural compliance score: Sep 88%, Oct 93%. Recurring findings: hold-door bag counts not signed (Sep, 7 turns); laterals not swept before cart closure on the evening bank (Sep 5 turns, Oct 2 turns); cart curtains left open (4 turns). Auditor's comment: 'Evening bank crews frequently receive late encode bags after carts are closed; crews have been instructed to radio for a hold where possible.' No comparison with the Quillon period is available.

catalogue.title: HBAA baggage reconciliation data by carrier and routing path, Harlow Bay departures, Jul–Oct
catalogue.source: Harlow Bay Airport Authority baggage reconciliation system
catalogue.text: HBAA baggage reconciliation extract, Harlow Bay departures, Jul–Oct. Bags not carried on the booked flight, per 1,000 departing passengers. Corvane: Jul 4.1, Aug 4.1, Sep 7.6, Oct 7.9. Pelion Airways (about 70% of Corvane's volume): 3.6, 3.8, 3.7, 3.6. Both carriers moved from Quillon to Tessaly on 1 Sep and are worked from Tessaly's single crew pool. Corvane by routing path: auto-read bags 3.9, 3.9, 3.8, 3.7; manual-encode bags 0.2, 0.2, 3.8, 4.2. Corvane bags diverted to manual encode, daily average: Aug 70, Sep 455, Oct 470. Evening-bank median encode dwell: Aug 7 min, Sep 29, Oct 33. Of the Corvane encode-path bags not carried, 91% reached the make-up lateral after its scheduled closing time. The check-in time profile of encode-path bags matches that of auto-read bags.

catalogue.title: HBAA sortation system maintenance log, tag reader arrays 1–4, Jul–Oct
catalogue.text: Planned maintenance: fortnightly lens cleaning on all four arrays, completed on schedule. Corrective work: 3 Sep, array 3: mounting bracket found loose after a cart strike; array realigned and returned to service the same shift. 19 Sep, array 2: one of six cameras replaced after an intermittent fault alarm. 11 Oct, array 1: firmware patch applied (vendor security update; read algorithm unchanged per release notes). The log records work performed. It does not record read rates.

catalogue.title: Corvane Harlow Bay departure schedule and baggage lateral times, Aug vs Sep–Oct
catalogue.text: Evening bank (17:00–21:00) departures: August 9 per day; from 1 Sep 11 per day (Corvane 418 and 422 added). Lateral opening: three hours before departure; lateral closing: 35 minutes before departure for all flights, unchanged. Two laterals (L5, L6) serve the evening bank; Corvane 418 and 422 share L6 with Corvane 410. Evening bank departing passengers, daily average: Aug 2,310; Sep 2,180; Oct 2,050. Daytime departures unchanged at 23 per day.

catalogue.title: Fennick Labels certificate of conformance and supplier cover letter, 4 Nov
catalogue.text: Certificate: batches FL-2207 to FL-2215 tested by Fennick's in-house laboratory against Corvane tag specification rev. 6; adhesive, tear strength and thermal sensitivity 'within specification'. Cover letter: 'Our stock is in use with several carriers without reported issues. Thermal media from different mills can require a modest increase in printer darkness. We would welcome a joint trial and are confident print quality will be resolved by adjusting your printer settings.' No third-party test results are attached.

catalogue.title: Teyra Systems technical bulletin TB-31 on thermal media settings for bag-tag printers
catalogue.text: General bulletin, issued 2023: 'Direct thermal media differ in activation energy. When changing media supplier, customers should print test tags and verify barcode grade before deployment. Low-sensitivity media may require darkness +2 to +4 and reduced print speed.' The bulletin names no media supplier and contains no data on Fennick or Brackwater stock. It also notes that print-head wear reduces barcode contrast.

catalogue.title: HBAA automatic tag reader statistics by tag range, arrays 1–4, 1 Aug–31 Oct
catalogue.source: Harlow Bay Airport Authority baggage systems (T. Rhee, engineer)
catalogue.text: HBAA automatic tag reader statistics, arrays 1–4, 1 Aug–31 Oct, by tag number range. No-read rate (bag diverted to manual encode): Corvane tags issued at Harlow Bay in August (Brackwater stock) 1.5%; issued Sep–Oct (Fennick stock) 11.8%, of which counters 11.5% and kiosks 12.0%. Corvane transfer tags issued at other stations 1.4%; Pelion tags 1.3%. Transfer and Pelion rates stay within 0.3 points on every array, including array 3 before and after its 3 Sep realignment. 14–16 Oct: Fennick stock ran short and counters 1–12 used Brackwater stock from stores; those tags failed at 1.6%, while kiosk tags issued the same days failed at 12.1%. Engineer's note (T. Rhee): sampled no-read images show faint, broken bars; the images cannot show whether the media or the printer heat setting is responsible.

catalogue.title: Interview notes with three Tessaly evening-bank crew leads, 7 Nov
catalogue.text: All three leads said the evening bank has been 'tight' since the two new departures and that they are short by one or two loaders on some nights. Lead A: 'We close the cart at minus 35 like we're told. Bags keep coming down after that and we get blamed.' Lead B said check-in 'sends us more rush bags than Quillon ever mentioned'. Lead C thought new staff were sometimes slow building containers. None of them could say how many bags arrived after closure.

catalogue.title: Corvane baggage service desk mishandling cause codes, Harlow Bay, Aug–Oct
catalogue.text: Cause codes are assigned by baggage service agents (Quillon staff in Aug, Tessaly staff from Sep) when a passenger reports a missing bag, before the bag is traced. Share of departing-bag mishandles, Aug/Sep/Oct: 'failure to load' 34%, 52%, 55%; 'late check-in' 14%, 9%, 8%; 'tagging error' 11%, 8%, 7%; 'transfer short-connection' 22%, 17%, 16%; 'other/unknown' 19%, 14%, 14%. Corvane's coding guide defines 'failure to load' as 'bag available at the lateral but not loaded'. Agents say the guide is 'rarely consulted'.

catalogue.title: HBAA manual encode desk staffing roster and rated throughput, Jul–Oct
catalogue.source: Harlow Bay Airport Authority baggage operations
catalogue.text: Manual encode desk, baggage hall level -1. Staffing: two encoders per shift on all shifts, July through October; no vacancy or sickness gap longer than one shift in any month. Rated throughput: about 22 bags per hour per encoder when the tag is partly legible, and 12 per hour when the bag must be matched by passenger name. The desk is staffed by HBAA, not by any ground handler. A third workstation exists and can be staffed with seven days' notice.

catalogue.title: Corvane–Tessaly handling agreement: SLA schedule and draft penalty calculation, Sep–Oct
catalogue.text: SLA 4.2: departing mishandled bags per 1,000 passengers not to exceed 4.5 in any month, measured on the Corvane dashboard. Exclusions cover 'causes outside the handler's reasonable control, including airport infrastructure'. The performance element is 8% of the monthly fee. Corvane finance's draft calculation puts the withholding for Sep and Oct at €186,000 in total. Clause 19: a breach notice triggers a 60-day cure period and allows Corvane to retender.

catalogue.title: Kiosk maintenance vendor service reports, Harlow Bay, Aug–Oct
catalogue.text: Callouts for kiosk tag-printer faults: Aug 14, Sep 31, Oct 29. Resolution recorded for each callout: 'media path cleared, test print OK'. Fault cause field: 'not determined' on 52 of the 60 Sep–Oct callouts and 'label debris on platen' on 8. Technicians did not record which tag stock was loaded. Preventive cleaning has been carried out fortnightly since 1 Sep under the revised contract.

catalogue.title: Harlow Bay weather and air traffic flow restriction summary, Aug–Oct
catalogue.source: Regional air navigation service and met office summary
catalogue.text: Days with flow restrictions affecting Harlow Bay departures: Aug 6, Sep 4, Oct 5. Thunderstorm ramp closures (lightning stop): Aug, 5 events totalling 6.2 hours; Sep, 2 events totalling 1.5 hours; Oct, none. Days with wind above loading limits: Oct 2. Restrictions applied to all carriers equally.

catalogue.title: Tessaly Ground mishandling performance at its other contracted airports, Jan–Oct
catalogue.text: Tessaly-supplied summary for four other airports where it has handled for more than two years: departing mishandled bags per 1,000 passengers stayed between 3.1 and 4.4 at every station in every month, with no rise in Sep–Oct. Tessaly notes that new-station start-ups 'typically see a small rise for six to eight weeks'. The figures are Tessaly's own and have not been verified by the customers concerned.

hypotheses.text: The changeover to Tessaly Ground put less experienced crews on Corvane's turns, and their handling failures are causing the rise in Corvane's mishandled-bag rate at Harlow Bay.

A change in how Corvane's bag tags are produced at Harlow Bay check-in has reduced automatic tag reading in the baggage system, and the extra bags diverted to manual encoding are missing their flights.
Corvane's added evening departures have compressed baggage handling on the evening bank enough to cause the rise in mishandled bags.
Deterioration of the airport baggage system's tag-scanning equipment has reduced automatic tag reading, and the extra bags diverted to manual encoding are missing their flights.
The tag stock supplied by Fennick Labels is defective as manufactured, so it would read poorly even with correctly adjusted printers.

edges.from: Handler changeover to Tessaly Ground on 1 Sep
edges.to: Rise in Corvane bags not carried on the booked flight

edges.from: Switch to Fennick Labels tag stock at Harlow Bay check-in on 1 Sep
edges.to: Rise in automatic tag-read failures for Corvane bags

edges.from: Rise in Corvane bags diverted to manual encoding
edges.to: Rise in Corvane bags not carried on the booked flight

edges.from: Switch to Fennick Labels tag stock at Harlow Bay check-in on 1 Sep

actions.text: Issue Tessaly Ground a formal breach notice and withhold the performance element of its fee for September and October.
Return Harlow Bay counters and kiosks to Brackwater tag stock now, while the Fennick stock is tested separately.
Lodge a formal defect claim with Fennick Labels seeking replacement of the delivered batches and recovery of mishandling costs.
Ask HBAA to staff an additional manual-encode workstation during the evening bank as a temporary measure.

truth.groundTruthNarrative: On 1 September four things changed at Harlow Bay at once. Tessaly Ground replaced Quillon as handler for both Corvane and Pelion. Corvane added two evening departures. Kiosk printer cleaning moved to fortnightly. And Corvane procurement switched every Harlow Bay counter and kiosk from Brackwater to cheaper Fennick tag stock. Corvane's departing mishandling rate rose from 4.1 to 7.6–7.9 per 1,000 passengers, and management blamed Tessaly's inexperienced crews. In fact, Fennick-printed tags fail automatic reading at about 12%, against about 1.5% for every other tag passing through the same arrays. When counters briefly went back to Brackwater stock (14–16 Oct), their no-read rate fell to 1.6% while kiosks still on Fennick stayed at 12%. The roughly six-fold rise in bags diverted to the unchanged two-person manual encode desk stretched evening dwell to about half an hour. Encode-path bags therefore reached laterals after closure and missed their flights. Corvane's auto-read bags showed no rise, and neither did Pelion's bags, which are worked by the same Tessaly crew pool. It is still unresolved whether Fennick stock is defective or simply needs different printer heat settings. The right step is to go back to Brackwater stock now. Penalising Tessaly would punish the wrong party.

answers.rationale: The initial file fits H1 well: the timing matches, 41% of staff are new, and both the manager and the VP blame the handler. C4 refutes it. Pelion moved to Tessaly on the same date, is worked by the same single crew pool, and its rate stayed flat (3.6–3.8). Corvane's auto-read bags, which crews load the same way, also stayed flat (3.9→3.7). The whole excess sits in encode-path bags, and 91% of those reached the lateral after its scheduled closing time, so they arrived too late for any crew to load them.

C9 shows the no-read rise is confined to Fennick-stock tags (11.8%), across both counters and kiosks. Other tags on the same arrays read normally, and the 14–16 Oct reversion to Brackwater brought counter tags back to 1.6%. C4 shows the resulting six-fold increase in encode-diverted bags, longer dwell, and encode-path bags arriving after lateral closure, while auto-read bags were unaffected. Together they establish the full chain. Neither item alone does: C4 cannot say why no-reads rose, and C9 cannot say that no-reads explain the missed flights.

If schedule compression were the cause, it would hit all evening bags, including auto-read ones. C4 shows Corvane's auto-read mishandling flat. The rise is confined to encode-path bags, whose volume rose from 70 to 455–470 a day while passengers fell, which two extra departures cannot explain. Check-in timing of encode-path bags matches auto-read bags.

C5's array repairs in September invite this explanation. But C9 shows transfer and Pelion tags reading at 1.3–1.4% within 0.3 points on every array, including array 3 before and after realignment, and Brackwater-stock tags read normally in October. Failing scanners would affect all tags.

Printer configuration was unchanged (E5), and Fennick stock fails on the same printers where Brackwater stock works (C9). That fits either a stock defect or a stock that needs higher printer heat. C9's engineer says the images cannot tell which. C7 (the supplier's own certificate, an interested source) and C8 (generic guidance) do not test the question. The claim is live but not established.

The evidence counts against the link itself. The same handler changeover, on the same date and with the same crews, left Pelion's rate flat and Corvane's auto-read rate flat. The excess bags missed flights because they reached the lateral after closure, which is not a crew loading failure. The C11 cause codes favouring 'failure to load' are assigned before tracing and are rarely checked against the definition.

Temporal order (switch on 1 Sep), specificity (only Fennick-range tags, at both counters and kiosks), the main rivals ruled out (same arrays read other tags normally; counters were not on the kiosk cleaning change) and a reversal (Brackwater at counters 14–16 Oct gave 1.6% while Fennick kiosks gave 12.1%) together establish causation.

Encode-diverted volume rose about six-fold, evening dwell rose from 7 to about 30 minutes, and 91% of the missed encode-path bags reached the lateral after scheduled closing. The encode-path mishandling rate rose from 0.2 to 3.8–4.2 while auto-read stayed flat. Check-in timing matches across paths, which rules out late check-in as a confounder.

Jam tickets rose from the same week the stock changed, so the two are associated. But kiosk preventive cleaning was halved on the same date, tickets are not split between kiosks and counters, and C14 records no cause for most callouts and no stock type. Causation is not established.

With H1 contradicted, a breach notice and fee withholding punish a handler whose crews are not causing the rise. It also starts a cure and retender process (C13) and leaves the tag problem untouched. It is damaging under H2 whichever way H5 turns out.

The October reversion showed Brackwater stock reads normally on the current printers. About five weeks of stock is in stores and the contract runs to 31 Dec (E5). Switching back removes the excess no-reads at source whether or not Fennick stock is defective, and it is easily reversed.

A defect claim would be justified if H5 were confirmed. But the evidence cannot yet separate defective stock from a printer-heat mismatch. If H5 is wrong, the claim is simply rejected and nothing lasting is lost.

Extra encode capacity would shorten evening dwell and reduce misses, so it is reasonable. But it treats the symptom, needs HBAA's cooperation, and becomes unnecessary once the stock is switched back. That makes it reasonable, not best.

With C4 and C9, the chain from Fennick stock to no-reads to encode backlog to missed flights is established, including a natural experiment. That is enough to commit to switching back to Brackwater stock. The open question in H5 does not affect that decision.

truth.authoringNotes: Trap: everything changed on 1 Sep, and leadership claims only the handler changed (E6). E4 and E5 quietly contradict that, which keeps the case fair. C4 is the contrast case: Pelion, with the same handler, crews and date, stayed flat, and Corvane's auto-read path stayed flat. Only C4 settles H1, H3, R1, R3 and A1. C9 is the only item that ties no-reads to the tag stock, rules out the scanners and includes a reversal; it settles R2 and H4. Neither item alone supports H2. Distractors: C5 (array repairs, a lure towards H4), C11 (pre-trace cause codes favouring 'failure to load'), C10 and C3 (mixed staff and handler accounts), C16 (Tessaly's own figures elsewhere), C7 and C8 (interested or generic vendor material that leaves H5 open), C12 (encode staffing, relevant to A4 only), C14 (does not resolve R4). Reviewer checks: H5 stays unknown because no catalogue item independently tests the stock at adjusted heat settings. R4 stays association-only because the cleaning change has the same date and the tickets are not split between kiosks and counters. A4 is not preferred because switching the stock back removes the backlog at source within days. No action other than A2 is keyed preferred. All numbers reconcile: E1 and C4 match, and C4's routing split sums to the totals.
